```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

symcompR has dense matrices of symbolic expressions with exact linear
algebra (determinants, inverses, row reduction, eigenvalues, and canonical
forms and decompositions), and symbolic matrix expressions in which a whole
matrix is a single symbol.

```{r}
library(symcompR)
x <- Symbol("x"); y <- Symbol("y")
a <- Symbol("a"); b <- Symbol("b"); c <- Symbol("c")
n <- Symbol("n", integer = TRUE)
```

## Building matrices

`Matrix()` takes a list of rows, an R matrix, a vector (which becomes a
column), or dimensions and a function of the row and column index.
Following R, indices start at 1 (SymPy starts at 0).

```{r}
M <- Matrix(list(list(1, 2), list(3, 4)))
M
Matrix(matrix(1:6, nrow = 2))
Matrix(c(1, 2, 3))
Matrix(2, 3, function(i, j) 10 * i + j)
```

Special matrices:

```{r}
eye(3)
zeros(2, 3)
ones(2, 2)
sym_diag(1, 2, 3)
jordan_cell(a, 3)
rot_axis3(sym_pi / 2)
```

`sym_diag()` is SymPy's `diag()`; it carries a prefix so that it does not
mask `base::diag()`.

## Indexing and shape

Matrices are indexed like R matrices, and assignment works the same way.

```{r}
M[1, 2]
M[2, ]
M[, 1]
dim(M)
M2 <- M
M2[1, 1] <- x
M2
```

`as.matrix()` converts a numeric symbolic matrix into an ordinary R matrix.

```{r}
as.matrix(M)
```

## Arithmetic

`+`, `-`, and multiplication by a scalar work as usual. Because `*` between
two R matrices is elementwise, the same holds here; the matrix product is
`%*%` and the matrix power `%^%`.

```{r}
M + M
2 * M
M * M
M %*% M
M %^% 2
M %^% -1
t(M)
```

Functions such as `subs()`, `diff()`, `N()`, and `simplify()` work entry by
entry, and `applyfunc()` applies any function to every entry.

```{r}
P <- Matrix(list(list(1, x), list(x^2, sin(x))))
subs(P, x, 2)
diff(P, x)
applyfunc(Matrix(list(list(sin(x)^2 + cos(x)^2, 1))), simplify)
N(Matrix(list(list(sqrt(S(2)), sym_pi))), 5)
```

## Determinant, inverse, and row reduction

```{r}
sym_det(M)
inverse(M)
S <- Matrix(list(list(a, b), list(c, 1)))
sym_det(S)
inverse(S)
adjugate(M)
cofactor(M, 1, 2)
permanent(M)
```

`sym_det()` uses Bareiss' fraction free elimination by default;
`method = "berkowitz"` and `method = "laplace"` are also available. A linear
system $Mx = v$ is solved with `solve()`:

```{r}
solve(M, Matrix(c(5, 6)))
```

`rref()` returns the reduced row echelon form and the pivot columns.
`rank_matrix()`, `nullspace()`, `columnspace()`, and `rowspace()` describe
the fundamental subspaces.

```{r}
S3 <- Matrix(list(list(1, 2, 3), list(4, 5, 6), list(7, 8, 9)))
rref(S3)
rank_matrix(S3)
nullspace(S3)
columnspace(S3)
sym_trace(S3)
```

## Eigenvalues and diagonalization

`charpoly()` gives the characteristic polynomial and `eigenvals()` its roots.
Exact eigenvalues can involve radicals.

```{r}
A <- Matrix(list(list(2, 1), list(1, 2)))
charpoly(A, x)
eigenvals(A)
eigenvals(M)
```

`eigenvects()` returns, for each eigenvalue, its algebraic multiplicity and a
basis of the eigenspace.

```{r}
ev <- eigenvects(A)
ev[[1]]$value
ev[[1]]$vectors[[1]]
is_diagonalizable(A)
```

`diagonalize()` returns `list(P, D)` with $A = P D P^{-1}$ and $D$
diagonal. The order of the eigenvalues on the diagonal is not
canonical, so the check below multiplies the factors back together.

```{r}
dg <- diagonalize(A)
dg$P %*% dg$D %*% inverse(dg$P) == A
sort(vapply(1:2, function(i) sstr(dg$D[i, i]), ""))
```

### Jordan normal form

Not every matrix is diagonalizable. `jordan_form()` returns `list(P, J)` with
$M = P J P^{-1}$ and $J$ in Jordan normal form.

```{r}
J3 <- Matrix(list(list(1, 1, 0), list(0, 1, 0), list(0, 0, 2)))
is_diagonalizable(J3)
jordan_form(J3)
K <- Matrix(list(list(5, 4, 2, 1), list(0, 1, -1, -1),
                 list(-1, -1, 3, 0), list(1, 1, -1, 2)))
jordan_form(K, calc_transform = FALSE)
```

The last matrix has eigenvalues 1, 2, and 4, with a 2 by 2 Jordan block for
the repeated eigenvalue 4.

`matrix_exp()` computes the matrix exponential of a diagonalizable matrix:

```{r}
matrix_exp(Matrix(list(list(0, 1), list(-1, 0))))
```

## Decompositions

```{r}
lu <- LUdecomposition(M)
lu$L
lu$U
qr <- QRdecomposition(M)
qr$Q
qr$R
SPD <- Matrix(list(list(4, 2), list(2, 3)))
cholesky(SPD)
LDLdecomposition(SPD)
```

Check one of them: $QR$ should give back $M$.

```{r}
simplify(qr$Q %*% qr$R)
```

## Integer normal forms

The Hermite normal form is the integer analogue of the reduced row echelon
form, and the Smith normal form diagonalizes an integer matrix by unimodular
row and column operations. Its diagonal, the invariant factors, classifies
finitely generated abelian groups.

```{r}
hermite_normal_form(Matrix(list(list(2, 7, 17, 29, 41),
                                list(3, 11, 19, 31, 43),
                                list(5, 13, 23, 37, 47))))
SN <- Matrix(list(list(12, 6, 4), list(3, 9, 6), list(2, 16, 14)))
smith_normal_form(SN)
invariant_factors(SN)
```

## Calculus with matrices

```{r}
jacobian(list(x^2 * y, 5 * x + sin(y)), list(x, y))
hessian(x^3 + x * y^2, list(x, y))
wronskian(list(sin(x), cos(x)), x)
gradient(x^2 * y, list(x, y))
```

## Vectors

Column vectors are one column matrices.

```{r}
u <- Matrix(c(1, 2, 3)); v <- Matrix(c(4, 5, 6))
dot(u, v)
cross(Matrix(c(1, 0, 0)), Matrix(c(0, 1, 0)))
norm_matrix(Matrix(c(3, 4)))
kronecker_product(M, eye(2))
```

## Matrix expressions

`MatrixSymbol(name, n, m)` is a matrix whose entries are not specified.
Products, sums, powers, transposes, and inverses of matrix symbols form
matrix expressions, which respect noncommutativity and check shapes.

```{r}
A <- MatrixSymbol("A", 2, 2); B <- MatrixSymbol("B", 2, 2)
A * B + A * B
A * B - B * A
t(A * B)
A^-1 * A
mat_shape(A * B)
```

Here `*` is the matrix product, because matrix symbols have no elementwise
interpretation; `HadamardProduct()` is the elementwise product.

```{r}
HadamardProduct(A, B)
MatrixElement(A, 0, 1)
as_explicit(A * B)
```

`MatrixElement()` uses SymPy's zero based indices, which is also how the
entries of an explicit matrix symbol print. `Trace()`, `Determinant()`, and
`Inverse()` are unevaluated until `doit()`.

```{r}
doit(Trace(A + B))
X <- MatrixSymbol("X", n, n)
X * Identity(n)
X + ZeroMatrix(n, n)
t(Inverse(X))
MatrixSlice(X, list(0, 2), list(0, 2))
```

Block matrices are built from matrix expressions.

```{r}
BlockMatrix(list(list(A, ZeroMatrix(2, 2)), list(ZeroMatrix(2, 2), B)))
```

More matrix expression classes. `MatAdd()`, `MatMul()`, and `MatPow()`
build unevaluated sums, products, and powers, `Transpose()` and `Adjoint()`
the (conjugate) transposes, `HadamardPower()` the elementwise power, and
`KroneckerProduct()` the Kronecker product. `matrix_symbols()` lists the
matrix symbols in an expression.

```{r}
C <- MatrixSymbol("C", 2, 2)
MatAdd(A, B)
MatMul(2, A, B)
MatPow(A, 3)
as_explicit(MatPow(A, 2))
Transpose(A * B)
doit(Transpose(A * B))
Adjoint(A)
HadamardPower(A, 2)
mat_shape(KroneckerProduct(A, B))
matrix_symbols(A * B)
doit(Determinant(A))
```

Structured matrices: `DotProduct()` of two column vectors, the diagonal of
a matrix (`DiagonalOf()`), a diagonal matrix from a matrix or vector
(`DiagonalMatrix()`, `DiagMatrix()`, `diagonalize_vector()`), the matrix of
ones, matrices defined by a function of the indices, permutation matrices,
and permuted rows (`MatrixPermute()`).

```{r}
u <- MatrixSymbol("u", 3, 1); w <- MatrixSymbol("w", 3, 1)
DotProduct(u, w)
doit(DotProduct(u, w))
as_explicit(DiagonalOf(A))
as_explicit(DiagonalMatrix(A))
as_explicit(DiagMatrix(u))
as_explicit(diagonalize_vector(u))
as_explicit(OneMatrix(2, 3))
as_explicit(FunctionMatrix(2, 2, Lambda(list(x, y), x + y)))
as_explicit(PermutationMatrix(Permutation(c(1, 2, 0))))
as_explicit(MatrixPermute(A, Permutation(c(1, 0))))
doit(Permanent(Matrix(list(list(1, 2), list(3, 4)))))
```

Block matrices: `BlockDiagMatrix()` is block diagonal, `block_collapse()`
evaluates block arithmetic, and `blockcut()` cuts a matrix into blocks.

```{r}
BlockDiagMatrix(A, B)
block_collapse(BlockMatrix(list(list(A, B))) * BlockDiagMatrix(B, C))
block_collapse(BlockDiagMatrix(A, B) + BlockDiagMatrix(B, C))
as_explicit(blockcut(Matrix(4, 4, f = 0:15), c(2, 2), c(2, 2)))
```

## More matrix functions

```{r}
M <- Matrix(list(list(1, 2), list(3, 4)))
transpose(M)
det_quick(M)
inv_quick(M)
per(M)
rowspace(Matrix(list(list(1, 2), list(2, 4))))[[1]]
set.seed(1)
randMatrix(2, 3)
cofactor_matrix(M)
minor(M, 1, 2)
trace_matrix(M)
is_square(M)
is_symmetric(M)
is_symmetric(Matrix(list(list(1, 2), list(2, 1))))
is_zero_matrix(zeros(2, 2))
vec(M)
hadamard_product(M, M)
matrix_multiply_elementwise(M, M)
diag_matrix(1, 2, 3)
adjoint(M)
pinv(Matrix(list(list(1, 2, 3))))
pinv(Matrix(list(list(1, 0), list(0, 2), list(0, 0))))
GramSchmidt(list(Matrix(list(1, 1, 0)), Matrix(list(1, 0, 1))))
GramSchmidt(list(Matrix(list(1, 1, 0)), Matrix(list(1, 0, 1))), orthonormal = TRUE)
```

`minor(M, i, j)` uses R's indices, starting at 1.

Sparse and banded matrices:

```{r}
SparseMatrix(2, 2, list(list(0, 0, 1), list(1, 1, 5)))
ImmutableSparseMatrix(2, 2, list(list(0, 1, 3)))
MutableSparseMatrix(2, 2, list(list(1, 0, 7)))
banded(3, list("0" = 1, "-1" = c(2, 3)))
```

Rotation matrices: `rot_axis1()` to `rot_axis3()` rotate the coordinate
frame, `rot_ccw_axis1()` to `rot_ccw_axis3()` rotate vectors
counterclockwise, and `rot_givens()` is a Givens rotation in a coordinate
plane.

```{r}
rot_axis1(sym_pi / 2)
rot_axis2(sym_pi / 2)
rot_ccw_axis1(sym_pi / 2)
rot_ccw_axis2(sym_pi / 2)
rot_ccw_axis3(sym_pi / 2)
rot_givens(0, 1, sym_pi / 3)
```

Linear systems and other constructions: `linear_eq_to_matrix()` returns
the coefficient matrix and right hand side as a tuple `(A, b)`, `casoratian()` is the
Casoratian of sequences (the discrete Wronskian), and `symarray()` is a
matrix of indexed symbols.

```{r}
k <- Symbol("k", integer = TRUE)
linear_eq_to_matrix(list(x + 2 * y - 3, 3 * x - y + 1), list(x, y))
casoratian(list(1, 2^k), k)
symarray("a", c(2, 2))
```

## Structured matrix expressions

`CompanionMatrix()` is the companion matrix of a monic polynomial, and
`DFT()` and `IDFT()` are the unitary discrete Fourier transform matrix and
its inverse. `MatrixUnit(rows, cols, i, j)` has a single one in position
`(i, j)`, with zero based indices as in SymPy.

```{r}
as_explicit(CompanionMatrix(Poly(x^3 + 2 * x + 5, x)))
as_explicit(DFT(2))
as_explicit(IDFT(2))
as_explicit(MatrixUnit(2, 2, 0, 1))
```

The factors of a matrix factorization are matrix expressions of their own:
`LofLU()` and `UofLU()`, `LofCholesky()` and `UofCholesky()`, `QofQR()` and
`RofQR()`, `EigenValues()` and `EigenVectors()`, and `UofSVD()`,
`SofSVD()` and `VofSVD()`. The functions `mat_lu()`, `mat_qr()`,
`mat_eig()` and `mat_svd()` return all the factors at once.

```{r}
k <- Symbol("k")
Xk <- MatrixSymbol("X", k, k)
LofLU(Xk)
mat_shape(UofLU(Xk))
LofCholesky(Xk)
UofCholesky(Xk)
QofQR(Xk)
RofQR(Xk)
EigenValues(Xk)
EigenVectors(Xk)
UofSVD(Xk)
SofSVD(Xk)
VofSVD(Xk)
do.call(Tuple, mat_lu(Xk))
do.call(Tuple, mat_qr(Xk))
do.call(Tuple, mat_eig(Xk))
do.call(Tuple, mat_svd(Xk))
```

`GenericIdentity()` and `GenericZeroMatrix()` are an identity and a zero
matrix of unspecified size. `hadamard_power()` is the elementwise power,
`combine_kronecker()` combines sums and products of Kronecker products, and
`ElementwiseApplyFunction()` applies a scalar function to every entry.

```{r}
Pk <- MatrixSymbol("P", k, k); Qk <- MatrixSymbol("Q", k, k)
GenericIdentity()
GenericZeroMatrix()
Pk * GenericIdentity()
hadamard_power(Pk, 2)
combine_kronecker(kronecker_product(Pk, Qk) + kronecker_product(Qk, Qk))
combine_kronecker(kronecker_product(Pk, Qk) * kronecker_product(Qk, Xk))
ElementwiseApplyFunction(sin, Xk)
as_explicit(ElementwiseApplyFunction(exp, MatrixSymbol("Y", 2, 2)))
```

`MatrixSet(n, m, set)` is the set of `n` by `m` matrices with entries in
`set`; `matrix_set_contains()` tests membership.

```{r}
M22 <- MatrixSet(2, 2, Reals)
M22
matrix_set_contains(M22, Matrix(list(list(1, 2), list(3, 4))))
matrix_set_contains(M22, Matrix(list(list(1, 2), list(3, sym_I))))
```

`dotprodsimp()` is the light simplification that matrix routines apply to
the intermediate sums of products:

```{r}
dotprodsimp(x / (x - 1) - 1 / (x - 1))
```

## Derivatives of matrix expressions

`diff()` differentiates a scalar or matrix valued matrix expression with
respect to a matrix symbol. A scalar function such as a trace has a matrix
derivative; a matrix valued function has a derivative of rank four, written
as an array expression (see the arrays and tensors vignette).
`matrix_derive()` does the same and converts the result back to matrix form
where possible.

```{r}
diff(Trace(Xk^2), Xk)
diff(Trace(Pk * Xk * Qk), Xk)
matrix_derive(Trace(Pk * Xk), Xk)
matrix_derive(t(Xk) * Pk * Xk, Xk)
```
